section: 3 · The pipe |> — the symbol you’ll type more than any other (15 min)
text:
3 · The pipe |> — the symbol you’ll type more than any other (15 min)






ImportantRead this one out loud



|> means “and then.” Take the thing on the left, hand it to the function on the right. That’s it. Everything from Monday on — every ETV cycle, every plot, every summary — is a chain of and thens.


LM6 — the same code, two ways (5 min). Question: on average, how warm were the July days? Without the pipe, you read this inside-out, from the deepest parentheses to the outermost:

# LM6a: nested — read from the INSIDE out
round(mean(airquality$Temp[airquality$Month == 7]), 1)

[1] 83.9


With the pipe, you read it top-to-bottom, like a recipe:

# LM6b: piped — read "and then", top to bottom
airquality$Temp[airquality$Month == 7] |>
  mean() |>
  round(1)

[1] 83.9


Same answer. But the second one you can say: “take July’s temperatures, and then average them, and then round to one decimal.”






NoteHow the pipe works — the one rule




x |> f() is exactly f(x). The left side becomes the first argument of the function on the right
x |> f(y) is f(x, y) — extra arguments go where they always did
So airquality$Temp |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) is mean(airquality$Temp, na.rm = TRUE)
Keyboard: Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + M types |> for you in Positron
Style: one step per line, indent the continuation. Your eye follows the recipe



LM7 — a real chain (4 min). Which days are missing Ozone? Read each line as “and then”:

# LM7: WHICH rows are missing Ozone? — read it as a sentence
airquality$Ozone |>
  is.na() |>
  which() |>
  head()

4 · How big is data? (13 min)
LM8 — the ladder (4 min). Data size is measured in bytes — one byte is roughly one letter. Every step up the ladder multiplies by a thousand:



Each step is ×1,000. A byte is a letter; a kilobyte is a paragraph; a megabyte is a photo; a gigabyte is an hour of video; a terabyte is a whole laptop.


LM9 — where real things land (4 min). The bars below are on a log scale — each gridline is another ×1,000. Notice where your laptop’s memory sits, because that’s the ceiling for what R can hold:



Real-world sizes on a log scale, from one letter to a national census. The orange “laptop memory” bar is the amount of data R can hold at once.










Unit
≈ bytes
Something you own that’s about that size




byte
1
one letter of a text message


kilobyte (KB)
1 thousand
a long email; this class’s survey as a .csv; airquality (5.6 KB)


megabyte (MB)
1 million
one phone photo (3 MB); one song (4 MB); a year of CA crime data (~100 MB)


gigabyte (GB)
1 billion
an hour of HD Netflix (3 GB); your laptop’s memory (8–16 GB)


terabyte (TB)
1 trillion
two of your laptop’s drives; a full US census extract


petabyte (PB)
1 quadrillion
Netflix’s entire catalog; the data behind a weather forecast



Now measure our objects:

# LM9: how big are OUR objects?
object.size(airquality)

5632 bytes

object.size(iris)

7256 bytes

7208 bytes

Why it matters (3 min): R holds data in memory — the orange bar, not the red one. A 2 GB file on an 8 GB laptop imports (barely); a 200 GB file does not — you’d need different tools (a database, or a bigger machine). File size is the first thing to check before importing, which is exactly where next week begins.

title: Foundations 02 — Data Types and Data Structures
text:
0 · The one distinction (4 min)

Type = what a single value is (number? text? TRUE/FALSE?). Structure = the container holding many values (vector? data frame? list?).

Everything today hangs off that sentence.
You already know how to insert a chunk (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + I, from last week). Whenever you see “➕ insert a chunk”, make one — every YT today depends on it.

title: Foundations 02 — Data Types and Data Structures
text:
1 · Data types (30 min)

1.1 · The types, defined first (before any code) (5 min)
Every single value in R has a type. Here are the ones you’ll live with, each with a Cal Poly example:








Type
What it is
Example value




numeric (double)
a number that can have decimals
4.75 — a latte at Julian’s


integer
a whole number (written with an L)
38L — people in the Rec Center at 7 am


character
text, in quotes
"Scout Coffee"


logical
TRUE or FALSE
TRUE — the drink is iced


factor
text from a fixed menu of allowed values
"morning" from {morning, afternoon, evening}


Date / date-time
a calendar date; a date and clock time
2026-09-22 / 2026-09-22 07:00:00


NA
a missing value — a hole, not a type of its own
the headcount nobody recorded

1 · Editor — the big middle area where this .qmd file is open. Code you keep lives here.
2 · Console — bottom of the screen, the tab labeled CONSOLE. R answers here, one command at a time. Code you type here is not saved.
3 · Variables — right side, under the SESSION tab. Every object you create this session shows up here. (Right now it says No variables have been created — remember what that looks like.)
4 · Plots — right side, below Variables. Pictures appear here.

R runs inside a session — a running copy of R that Positron is talking to.
How to get to the Session tab. Look at the top-right corner of Positron (arrow 6 in the picture). It shows which R is running, something like R 4.5.1. That label is your session. It has memory. Every object you create lives in the session, and shows up in Variables.
It can be restarted. The Restart button (top-right session menu, or the Console toolbar) wipes the session’s memory clean — Variables empties out. Your files are untouched.
It can be replaced. The same menu lets you pick a different R (or Python) if more than one is installed. Don’t do that today; just know the button exists.

The Session 6 min
R runs inside a session — a running copy of R that Positron is talking to.
How to get to the Session tab. Look at the top-right corner of Positron (arrow 6 in the picture). It shows which R is running, something like R 4.5.1. That label is your session. Click it once: a small menu opens showing the running R, a Restart button, a Shutdown button, and any other interpreters installed on your computer. Close the menu (press Escape). Now look just below it on the right side: the panel labeled SESSION holds the Variables and Plots panes — everything the session is holding in memory, made visible.
Three things to know about the session, today:

It has memory. Every object you create lives in the session, and shows up in Variables.
It can be restarted. The Restart button (top-right session menu, or the Console toolbar) wipes the session’s memory clean — Variables empties out. Your files are untouched.
It can be replaced. The same menu lets you pick a different R (or Python) if more than one is installed. Don’t do that today; just know the button exists.

Do this now: create nothing yet, look at Variables (empty), and remember what empty looks like — we’ll come back after we’ve made some objects.

1.1 · The types, defined first (before any code) 5 min
Every single value in R has a type. Here are the ones you’ll live with, each with a Cal Poly example:








Type
What it is
Example value




numeric (double)
a number that can have decimals
4.75 — a latte at Julian’s


integer
a whole number (written with an L)
38L — people in the Rec Center at 7 am


character
text, in quotes
"Scout Coffee"


logical
TRUE or FALSE
TRUE — the drink is iced


factor
text from a fixed menu of allowed values
"morning" from {morning, afternoon, evening}


Date / date-time
a calendar date; a date and clock time
2026-09-22 / 2026-09-22 07:00:00


NA
a missing value — a hole, not a type of its own
the headcount nobody recorded









ImportantTeaching note — definitions before class()




Read the table row by row before anyone runs code. The order today is: define the type → then discover it with class()
Ask: “If I write a latte price, which row?” (numeric) “The name of the shop?” (character) “Whether it’s iced?” (logical)
NA gets one sentence: it’s a placeholder for “nobody knows,” and it can sit inside any type

1.3 · Three families: quantitative, categorical, other 6 min
R’s types sort into three families you’ll use to pick plots and summaries all term:









Family
Question it answers
R types
Cal Poly examples




Quantitative
how much? how many? — you can average it
numeric, integer
latte price (4.75), Rec Center headcount (38), miles from campus (2.3)


Categorical
which kind? which group? — you count it
character, factor, logical
coffee shop ("Julian's", "Starbucks", "Scout"), time slot ("morning"), iced (TRUE)


Other (time/date)
when? — ordered, but not a plain number
Date, date-time
the day you bought the latte, the clock time you swiped into the Rec




Q2. Which family: (a) the number of people in the Rec Center at 5 pm · (b) the shop that made your latte · (c) the date of the game vs. UCSB · (d) whether you bought a latte today (yes/no)?
Your answer: (a) quantitative · (b) categorical · (c) other — a date · (d) categorical — a logical is a two-level category.







TipQ2 answer + why the families matter




Q2 (a) quantitative (b) categorical (c) other / date (d) categorical — logical is a yes/no category
Why bother: quantitative → histograms and means; categorical → bar charts and counts; dates → line plots over time. Week 3’s plots pick themselves once you name the family
Trap to name now: a number can be categorical. Your student ID is digits, but averaging student IDs is nonsense



A small distinction — “string” vs “character”. Other languages call text a string. R calls the type character, and one piece of text ("Scout Coffee") is a string — a character value of length one. So "latte" is a string, its class is character, and c("latte", "mocha") is a character vector of two strings. You’ll hear both words; they are not in conflict.


1.4 · Factors vs characters — why it matters 6 min
LM4 — the same text, two types (4 min). Rec Center headcounts come with a time slot. As character, the slots are just words; as a factor, they come with a fixed menu of allowed values (levels) in an order you choose:

# LM4: character vs factor
slot_chr <- c("evening", "morning", "afternoon", "morning", "evening", "evening")
slot_fct <- factor(slot_chr, levels = c("morning", "afternoon", "evening"))

class(slot_chr)

[1] "character"

class(slot_fct)

[1] "factor"

levels(slot_fct)

[1] "morning"   "afternoon" "evening"  

table(slot_chr)   # alphabetical — afternoon first

slot_chr
afternoon   evening   morning 
        1         3         2 

table(slot_fct)   # the order YOU chose — morning first

slot_fct
  morning afternoon   evening 
        2         1         3 



Q3. How many levels does slot_fct have, and what order did we give them? Why would that order matter on a bar chart?
Your answer: 3 levels — morning, afternoon, evening. A bar chart follows the levels, so the factor plots the day in time order; the character version plots alphabetically (afternoon, evening, morning), which reads as nonsense.







TipQ3 answer — the two reasons factors exist




Q3 3 levels, in the order morning → afternoon → evening
Reason 1 — order. Characters sort alphabetically; factors sort by your levels. Every plot and table of a categorical variable inherits that order
Reason 2 — a fixed menu. A factor knows "night" is not allowed (it becomes NA); a character column will happily accept "Morning", "morning ", and "AM" as three different groups. Factors are how you catch typos in categories
Rule of thumb to leave them with: character = free text (names, comments); factor = a category with a known set of values
The menu metaphor pays rent in week 6 when forcats arrives

text:
3 · The pipe |> — the symbol you’ll type more than any other 15 min






ImportantRead this one out loud



|> means “and then.” Take the thing on the left, hand it to the function on the right. That’s it. Everything from Monday on — every ETV cycle, every plot, every summary — is a chain of and thens.


LM6 — the same code, two ways (5 min). Question: on average, how warm were the July days? Without the pipe, you read this inside-out, from the deepest parentheses to the outermost:

# LM6a: nested — read from the INSIDE out
round(mean(airquality$Temp[airquality$Month == 7]), 1)

[1] 83.9


With the pipe, you read it top-to-bottom, like a recipe:

# LM6b: piped — read "and then", top to bottom
airquality$Temp[airquality$Month == 7] |>
  mean() |>
  round(1)

[1] 83.9


Same answer, 83.9°F. But the second one you can say: “take July’s temperatures, and then average them, and then round to one decimal.”






NoteHow the pipe works — the one rule




x |> f() is exactly f(x). The left side becomes the first argument of the function on the right
x |> f(y) is f(x, y) — extra arguments go where they always did
So airquality$Temp |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) is mean(airquality$Temp, na.rm = TRUE)
Keyboard: Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + M types |> for you in Positron (if it types %>%, that’s the older tidyverse pipe — same idea; set the native pipe option in Positron’s settings)
Style: one step per line, indent the continuation. Your eye follows the recipe

1.1 · The types, defined first (before any code) 5 min
Every single value in R has a type. Here are the ones you’ll live with, each with a Cal Poly example:








Type
What it is
Example value




numeric (double)
a number that can have decimals
4.75 — a latte at Julian’s


integer
a whole number (written with an L)
38L — people in the Rec Center at 7 am


character
text, in quotes
"Scout Coffee"


logical
TRUE or FALSE
TRUE — the drink is iced


factor
text from a fixed menu of allowed values
"morning" from {morning, afternoon, evening}


Date / date-time
a calendar date; a date and clock time
2026-09-22 / 2026-09-22 07:00:00


NA
a missing value — a hole, not a type of its own
the headcount nobody recorded









ImportantTeaching note — definitions before class()




Read the table row by row before anyone runs code. The order today is: define the type → then discover it with class()
Ask: “If I write a latte price, which row?” (numeric) “The name of the shop?” (character) “Whether it’s iced?” (logical)
NA gets one sentence: it’s a placeholder for “nobody knows,” and it can sit inside any type

[1] "integer"

[1] "character"

[1] "logical"



Q1. Predictions: numeric · integer · character · logical

Q6. Your laptop has 8 GB of memory. Roughly how many copies of a 500 MB dataset could fit at once (ignore overhead)? About 16 — 8 GB ≈ 8,000 MB, and 8,000 / 500 = 16. How many hours of HD video is that? Not even three.

honest version: overhead means fewer in practice; R also copies objects when you modify them
the point is order-of-magnitude reasoning, which is sub-outcome 1.12’s whole job
